title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to measure whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We present the sealed design, deterministic execution accounting, representative validator traces, contamination‑check evidence (Mininet holdout = 20 tasks; zero disagreements), artifact‑grounded interpretation, and threats to validity and reproducibility (including one documented missing labeled artifact: the explicit random seed label for the Mininet holdout).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational productivity gains for network operations (NetOps) but creates risk: incorrect or unsafe changes can cause outages, policy violations, or degraded service. Because of these risks, many architectures combine LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) so that unsafe candidates can be detected and corrected before application. The marginal operational value of automated repair depends on (i) the baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures produced by the chosen generator and prompt policy; (ii) the validator’s coverage and fidelity; and (iii) the repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question and executed it under a sealed design: Does a deterministic GVR pipeline that uses a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline, holding the generated candidate fixed (shared initial generation), on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?
sections.related_work: Prior work documents LLM factual errors, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism across domains and proposes mitigation patterns relevant to NetOps: grounding (retrieval‑augmented generation), verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded/guarded agent architectures. Prototype NetOps systems and intent→configuration tools show feasibility but often lack external, instrumented failure‑rate studies. Architectures integrating LLM generation with deterministic network validators (e.g., Batfish‑style checkers) and repair loops are advocated to improve safety; red‑team audits and configuration‑brittleness studies demonstrate that tool‑description injection and agentic tool chaining can materially change safety outcomes and expand attack surface. These prior findings motivate externally auditable, preregistered measurements that isolate the marginal effect of adding deterministic repair for a fixed model and prompt policy. We cite representative survey and prototype records that established these motivations and informed our preregistered estimand and contamination handling (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The study was preregistered (study_id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) with a paired design, n = 200 tasks, and a single pre‑registered primary inferential test: exact McNemar two‑sided (α = 0.05) on paired binary pass/fail outcomes (LLM‑only vs GVR applied to the same generated candidate). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; confidence intervals were computed via bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Power planning assumed a baseline unsafe incidence ≈ 30% and targeted a 50% relative reduction; the design and stopping rules (max model calls = 400; at most 1 repair call per task) were frozen before any model calls and archived in the preregistration artifact.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks spanning four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and expected final states, explicit workflow constraints (e.g., make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields), and a required_sequence that the primary deterministic checker enforces. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered and applied as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to flag validator–emulator mismatches. The run executed that holdout and recorded the contamination_summary artifact reporting zero disagreements.

Model, adapter, and shared‑initial semantics. The experiment used the hosted model declared in the preregistration (gpt‑5‑mini) invoked through the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Crucially, the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task a single initial candidate was generated deterministically and reused for both the baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This isolates the marginal effect of validator+repair on the same generator output and removes per‑condition sampling variance. The adapter accounting records hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming shared reuse across conditions.

Repair policy, budgets, and contamination handling. The preregistered repair policy allowed one automated repair prompt to the same LLM when the primary validator reported violations; up to 200 repair calls were therefore allowed but only if initial candidates failed validation. The contamination_plan deterministically excluded tasks where primary validator vs emulator disagreed; three deterministic sensitivity analyses were preregistered to examine robustness if flags occurred (none were triggered in this run). Missingness and exclusion rules were fixed in the preregistration and applied deterministically during execution.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcome. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes (planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400) and retained complete_pair_count = 200. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair_calls_used = 0. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) show baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Confirmatory inference. With zero discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand the prespecified ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is logically untestable on this sample because there were no baseline validator failures for GVR to reduce.

Representative artifacts and diagnostics. Representative task artifacts (pair‑000001 through pair‑000006) show shared initial generator outputs that precisely matched the task required_sequence and passed validation: validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0 in each representative record. Representative difficulty annotations (examples: make_before_break_uplink_switchover; paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) and parsed_command_count/required_command_count are recorded in validator traces and confirm that the task bank contained medium→very_hard workflow constraints despite producing validator‑satisfying candidates.

Contamination check and emulator holdout. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed; analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports zero validator–emulator disagreements. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts record all consistency checks passed (marginal_contingency_consistent = true, pair_accounting_consistent = true, episode_accounting_consistent = true). Provider call audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, and cache_hit_count = 0, consistent with the shared_initial design.

Unexecuted branches and secondary estimands. Planned secondary estimands (average repair iterations, model‑call cost per successful repair, GVR‑introduced failure rate) remain unpopulated because no repair attempts occurred; secondary_results in the analysis bundle are empty. Several preregistered sensitivity checks were not invoked because no tasks were flagged and no episodes failed.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation and operational implication. The observed degenerate confirmatory outcome demonstrates a simple logical point: when the chosen model, prompt policy, and adapter produce validator‑passing candidates for all items in a workload, a validator‑coupled repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This null result is tightly scoped: it does not imply that GVR is never useful. Rather, it clarifies that GVR’s marginal operational benefit is conditional on baseline validator failure prevalence and on validator coverage and fidelity. Practitioners planning automated repair should therefore first measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workloads and exercise validator coverage with end‑to‑end emulation; when baseline failures are rare, resources are usually better invested in improving validator fidelity (device semantics, vendor idiosyncrasies), adversarial testing, multi‑sample or multi‑model generation, or human‑in‑the‑loop decision points.

Why baseline failures were zero in this run. Artifact‑grounded reasons include: (1) the prompt template and deterministic shared_initial generation policy produced candidates that conformed to the explicit task‑bank constraints; (2) the curated task bank encodes clear required_sequences that directly map to the validator checks and therefore may be easier for a deterministic prompt policy to satisfy; (3) the deterministic primary validator enforces the task‑encoded constraints but may omit device‑level or vendor idiosyncratic behaviors only visible under full data‑plane emulation or hardware; and (4) the single repair budget combined with shared_initial design removed per‑condition resampling as a pathway to generate alternative repairable candidates.

Reproducibility and a documented artifact gap. All key execution artifacts (model‑call logs, validator traces, paired contingency tables, bootstrap parameters, and deterministic reconciliation files) are archived and referenced in the analysis bundle. The contamination summary confirms execution of the Mininet holdout (20 tasks) and reports zero disagreements. One remaining reproducibility gap must be disclosed: the explicit labeled artifact recording the randomized selection seed for the Mininet holdout is absent from the archived bundle, which prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination_summary evidence that no disagreements were observed. We report this gap transparently as required by the preregistration and disclosure rules.

Threats to validity and future directions. Internal validity: preregistration, deterministic adapter enforcement, and frozen stopping rules protect against post‑hoc design changes; however, shared_initial design trades generality for control and specifically removes per‑condition sampling variance. Construct validity: the primary validator checks task‑encoded constraints but can miss device‑level idiosyncrasies and emergent failure modes only detectable via richer emulation or real hardware. External validity: the experiment used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), a single sampling policy (shared initial), and a curated task bank; results may differ with other models, nonzero temperature sampling, multiple draws, larger repair budgets, adversarial tasks, or production workloads. Conclusion validity: with zero discordant pairs the planned McNemar test is uninformative for the preregistered target effect; nevertheless reporting the zero‑failure outcome is scientifically useful for future workload selection and power planning. Future experiments that would meaningfully evaluate GVR’s efficacy should (a) target workloads with nontrivial baseline validator failure prevalence, (b) increase repair budgets and permit multi‑step repair, (c) evaluate per‑condition resampling or multi‑model ensembles, and (d) extend validator fidelity with richer emulator or hardware checks.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was not testable on this task bank because the baseline failure rate was 0%. This artifact‑grounded null outcome clarifies a practical point: the marginal value of automated repair is workload dependent. We archive all execution and analysis artifacts for independent inspection and recommend that future work measure baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage on representative or adversarial workloads before assessing automated repair investments.

Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared_initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls; preregistration artifact SHA‑256 is archived with the execution manifest. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds (where archived), validator traces, emulator traces, logs, deterministic reconciliation, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts show shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
